al-Andalusiyyun (the Andalusians, in North African usage for the exiles)

summary: The Moriscos were the Muslims of the Spanish kingdoms who were compelled to accept Christian baptism, in Granada (1499-1501) and Castile (1502) and in Valencia and Aragon (1521-1526), together with their descendants, until their expulsion in 1609-1614. Historians describe among them a range of religious identities, from clandestine Islamic practice (crypto-Islam), for which a North African fatwa of 1504 offered juristic justification, to sincere Catholicism.
description:
Morisco, a Castilian diminutive of moro ('Moor'), was the name Old Christians gave to baptized Muslims and their descendants; official usage also called them New Christians of Moors. The community was created by compulsion, though the Crown and its advisers held the baptisms canonically valid. After the breach of the Capitulations of Granada, the Muslims of that kingdom were baptized in 1499-1501, and a royal pragmatic of February 1502 required the remaining Muslims of the Crown of Castile to accept baptism or leave. In the Crown of Aragon, where Muslim vassals were numerous in Valencia and Aragon, many Muslims of Valencia were baptized during the Germanías revolt in the summer of 1521; in 1525 Charles V, advised by an assembly of jurists and theologians, decreed those baptisms valid and the converts bound to the Catholic faith, and the Valencian jurist and inquisitorial prosecutor Fernando de Loazes argued in a treatise of the same year that they were valid under the canonists' doctrine on forced baptism, as Isabelle Poutrin describes; decrees of 1525-1526 then ended the legal practice of Islam in Valencia and Aragon. The resulting population was diverse: largely Arabic-speaking in Granada and Valencia, largely Romance-speaking in Aragon and Castile, and spread across peasant, artisan, and in Granada noble milieus. As baptized Christians the Moriscos fell under the jurisdiction of the Inquisition, whose trial records are a principal source for their history. In Granada a pragmatic of 1567 banned the use of Arabic and of Moorish dress and customs; the Morisco nobleman Francisco Núñez Muley protested it in a memorandum to the president of the royal Audiencia, a rare surviving statement in a Morisco's own voice, and the second revolt of the Alpujarras (1568-1571) that followed ended with the dispersal of the Granadan Moriscos across Castile.

The religious-legal situation of Muslims under Christian rule had long been debated by Maliki jurists of the Maghrib and al-Andalus, on the paradigm of the Prophet's emigration (hijra) from Mecca. Its best-known statement is the fatwa Asna al-matajir of Ahmad al-Wansharisi (d. 914/1508), completed, by its own colophon, on 19 Dhu l-Qa'da 896 (1491) in answer to a question about Andalusian emigrants in the Maghrib who regretted having left. The question itself states that the aim of emigration is 'the safety of religion, family, and children' and leaving the rule of the unbelieving community for that of the Muslim community. Al-Wansharisi answers that 'emigration from the land of unbelief to the land of Islam is an obligation until the Day of Resurrection' (al-hijra min ard al-kufr ila ard al-Islam farida ila yawm al-qiyama), that it lapses only for those unable to emigrate in every way, citing Q 4:97-99, and, quoting Ibn Rushd al-Jadd, that a Muslim may not remain where 'the rulings of the polytheists apply to him' (tajri 'alayhi ahkam al-mushrikin). Devin Stewart characterizes this as the majority Maliki position; Jocelyn Hendrickson nuances the reading, arguing that al-Wansharisi's primary audience was his fellow Maghribi jurists and that the Portuguese-occupied Maghrib was chiefly in view. Against this background stands the text issued in Rajab 910/December 1504 by Ahmad ibn Abi Jum'a al-Maghrawi al-Wahrani (d. 917/1511), known as 'the Mufti of Oran', whom Stewart identifies as a jurist from Oran who settled in Fez and probably wrote it there, in opposition to al-Wansharisi's view (one Aljamiado version gives the date as Rajab 909). Hendrickson suggests, tentatively, that it was 'unsolicited advice' rather than a fatwa, written in response to the community's appeal to the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II. Addressed to the Moriscos, it grants, as Stewart summarizes it, comprehensive dispensation to feign adherence to Christianity: under coercion they may drink wine or eat pork, pray with Christians, utter Christian creeds, or even insult the Prophet (since the Christians pronounce his name 'Mamad', the text advises intending by it the devil or another bearer of that name), and may dispense with the ordinary forms of ablution and prayer, so long as they inwardly reject these acts and hold that the underlying obligations still stand. It survives in one Arabic copy and three Aljamiado versions, copied as late as 1563 and 1609, which Stewart takes as evidence of its importance to the community; Harvey, as quoted by Stewart, calls it 'the key theological document for the study of Spanish Islam' in this period. The classical scriptural ground for such dispensation is the Qur'anic exemption of 'those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith' (Q 16:106), the locus classicus of the legal doctrine of coercion (ikrah), and Q 3:28, from which the term taqiyya ('precautionary dissimulation') is usually derived. Whether the Moriscos' practice is properly called taqiyya is itself debated: L. Sabbagh holds that taqiyya matters chiefly to sectarian groups and that Sunnis disfavour it as dangerous to the moral life of the community; J.-P. Molénat notes that the fatwa does not use the term; María Jesús Rubiera Mata, concurring, calls the fatwa an anomaly among Iberian and North African fatwas on Muslims under Christian rule and holds taqiyya to be a Shi'i concept that Sunni Moriscos would not have recognized; and Stewart argues that dissimulation under coercion was doctrinally available to Sunnis and was discussed in the Sunni exegesis, hadith, and legal works known to Maghribi and Andalusi jurists, noting that al-Wansharisi himself uses the term in his notarial manual.

Morisco religious culture is known above all through Aljamiado literature: Romance (chiefly Aragonese and Castilian) written in Arabic script, comprising Qur'an translations and commentary, legal and ritual manuals, prophetic legends, and polemic, produced mainly among the Romance-speaking Mudejars and Moriscos of Aragon. Its best-known author is the anonymous 'Young Man of Arévalo' (Mancebo de Arévalo), a Castilian settled in Aragon who wrote in the first half of the sixteenth century; his Tafsira draws, according to Bernabé Pons's review of Narváez's edition, on Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ and on La Celestina for an Islamic devotional purpose. The Lead Books of the Sacromonte, Arabic texts on a parchment found in 1588 in the minaret of Granada's old Friday Mosque and on lead tablets found in the caves of the Valparaíso hill from 1595, presented themselves as early Christian revelation and were condemned by the papacy in 1682; modern scholarship treats them as productions of Morisco circles, which Pieter van Koningsveld and Gerard Wiegers count among the Moriscos' last literary works and which Mercedes García-Arenal and Fernando Rodríguez Mediano read as a window onto the Morisco worldview.

Historians differ over how far the Moriscos remained Muslims. The closing part of the narrative quoted in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib, which reaches al-Maqqari's own time, states that those who remained, 'although Christians in appearance, were not so in their hearts; for they worshipped Allah in secret'. L. P. Harvey and Anwar Chejne describe a sustained crypto-Islam; Mary Elizabeth Perry argues that Morisco women preserved Islamic practice, language, and memory within the household; James Tueller, in a study titled Good and Faithful Christians, argues that many Moriscos were sincere Catholics; and Trevor Dadson, studying the 'Old Moriscos' (antiguos) of Villarrubia in the Campo de Calatrava, Castilian Mudejars converted in the early sixteenth century and their descendants, describes assimilation and peaceful coexistence with their Old Christian neighbours. This entry presents these as the attributed findings of historians, and does not decide which characterization fits the community as a whole.
editorial_notes: HOME TRADITION (ADR-0010): filed under islam because the entry chiefly concerns a community of Muslim origin and its religious life; this is a storage convention, not a claim of ownership. The Moriscos were baptized Christians in law, and their Christian identity, sincere or imposed, is part of the entry; the Christian institutional side (the Inquisition, conversion policy) is described from historians' accounts. MODELED as a concept rather than an event, like sephardic-diaspora, because it names a community and a religious-cultural formation lasting more than a century; the datable events (the fall of Granada and the conversions, the expulsion) are modeled as events. NEUTRALITY: the Islamic legal voice is represented on its own terms and attributed: al-Wansharisi's Asna al-matajir in its own words (read in the Arabic text), with 'majority position' given as Stewart's characterization and Hendrickson's reading of its audience and purpose given as her interpretation; and the Oran text in Stewart's summary, with Hendrickson's tentative view that it was 'unsolicited advice' attributed. The Christian theological-legal voice is represented by the 1525 validation of the Valencian baptisms and Loazes's canon-law argument, as analysed by Poutrin. The scholarly dispute over the term taqiyya (Sabbagh, Molénat, and Rubiera Mata against Stewart) is presented as a live debate without adjudication (neutrality #2). Christian characterizations of Moriscos as apostates or heretics belong to the sources of the period and are not adopted. The question of how far the Moriscos were Muslims or Christians is left open, with each view attributed (neutrality #1). SOURCING (neutrality #8, #9, #11): (a) modern academic historians (Harvey, Chejne, Perry, Tueller, Dadson, García-Arenal and Rodríguez Mediano, van Koningsveld and Wiegers, Hendrickson, López-Morillas); (b) primary texts in the Moriscos' own and their jurists' voices (al-Wansharisi's Asna al-matajir; the Oran fatwa through Stewart's studies and Harvey's translation; Núñez Muley's memorandum in Barletta's translation; the Mancebo de Arévalo's Tafsira in Narváez's edition; al-Maqqari's narrative), and the Qur'an; (c) a modern Muslim legal scholar, Khaled Abou El Fadl, on the juristic discourse on Muslim minorities. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE: Stewart's two open-access Al-Qantara articles were read directly for the passages used (the identity, date, place, and purpose of the Oran fatwa; its content; the taqiyya debate) and are rated high; Q 16:106 was read at quran.com and is rated high; the Asna al-matajir was read in the Arabic digital text (OpenITI, from Husayn Mu'nis's edition) for the question, the opening of the answer, the Ibn Rushd quotation, and the colophon, and is rated high for those passages; Caitlyn Olson's open-access review of Hendrickson was read directly and is rated high for its summary of Hendrickson's arguments; al-Maqqari's narrative was read directly (vol. 2, p. 391) and is rated high, as in the event entries; Poutrin's article was consulted through its published abstract only and is rated medium; Bernabé Pons's open-access review was read for the characterization of the Mancebo de Arévalo, and is used to verify the Narváez edition, which is rated medium because the edition itself was not consulted. All other sources were verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher, catalog, and review records but not read line by line, and are rated medium. The year range 1499-1614 runs from the first forced baptisms to the end of the expulsion; descendants in the North African diaspora are outside its scope.

historical_period.note: From the first forced baptisms in Granada (1499) to the completion of the expulsion (1614); the conversions in Castile (1502) and in Valencia and Aragon (1525-1526) fall within this range. Descendants of the exiles in North Africa and the Ottoman lands are outside the range.

relations.note: The Morisco community took shape in the forced conversions that followed the breach of the Capitulations of Granada (Granada 1499-1501, Castile 1502).
The Moriscos were expelled from the Spanish kingdoms by the decrees of Philip III between 1609 and 1614.
The Moriscos were descendants of the Muslim population of al-Andalus and of the Mudejars who lived under Christian rule; in North Africa the exiles were often called Andalusians.

Maliki jurists debating whether Muslims under Christian rule must emigrate to Muslim territory reasoned from the paradigm of the Prophet's emigration from Mecca to Medina: al-Wansharisi's Asna al-matajir (1491) held emigration obligatory, while the Oran fatwa of 1504 addressed those who remained.
The fatwas addressed to Mudejars and Moriscos, by al-Wansharisi and by Ibn Abi Jum'a al-Wahrani among others, were issued within the Maliki school of law, dominant in al-Andalus and the Maghrib.

The Oran fatwa of 1504 applied the doctrine, which jurists and exegetes ground in Q 16:106, that a believer who outwardly professes unbelief under coercion while the heart remains firm in faith is excused.

Historians' debates over coexistence in early modern Spain extend to the Moriscos: Trevor Dadson's study of the Old Moriscos of Villarrubia argues for coexistence and assimilation, a generalization that other historians of the expulsion resist.

Academic history of the Moriscos from the forced conversions to the expulsion, including crypto-Islam, a near-complete English translation of the Oran fatwa (pp. 60-63), and the Mancebo de Arévalo; the outside-scholarship lens. sources.citation: Stewart, Devin. 'The Identity of "the Muftī of Oran", Abū l-'Abbās Aḥmad b. Abī Jum'ah al-Maghrāwī al-Wahrānī (d. 917/1511).' Al-Qanṭara 27, no. 2 (2006): 265-301. doi:10.3989/alqantara.2006.v27.i2.2. Peer-reviewed article identifying the author of the 1504 fatwa to the Moriscos as a jurist from Oran who studied in Tlemcen and settled in Fez, arguing that he probably issued the fatwa in Fez in 910/1504 in opposition to al-Wansharisi, dating it to Rajab 910 (with the variant Rajab 909 in the Aljamiado version A), and describing its transmission in one Arabic copy (Vatican, discovered by Muhammad 'Abd Allah 'Inan in 1951) and three Aljamiado versions copied as late as 1563 and 1609. The abstract, introduction, and dating sections were read directly (open access).
sources.license: Open access, CC BY 4.0 (Al-Qanṭara, CSIC). Read directly for the passages cited.

sources.citation: Stewart, Devin. 'Dissimulation in Sunni Islam and Morisco Taqiyya' [La disimulación en el islam sunní y la taqiyya morisca]. Al-Qanṭara 34, no. 2 (2013): 439-490. doi:10.3989/alqantara.2013.016. Peer-reviewed article on the doctrine of dissimulation and coercion (ikrah) in Sunni exegesis, hadith, and law, with a summary of the content of the 1504 Oran fatwa, a survey of the scholarly debate over whether it endorses taqiyya (Sabbagh, Molénat, Rubiera Mata, who calls the fatwa an anomaly), quotation of Harvey's description of it as 'the key theological document for the study of Spanish Islam' (Harvey 2005, p. 60), the Qur'anic loci Q 3:28, 16:106, and 40:28, and al-Wansharisi's use of the term taqiyya in his notarial manual. The passages on the fatwa's content, the debate, the Qur'anic loci, and al-Wansharisi (pp. 443-444, 451-452, and the section on affidavits) were read directly (open access).
sources.license: Open access (Al-Qanṭara, CSIC). Read directly for the passages cited.

sources.citation: The Qur'an, Q 16:106, read at quran.com in The Clear Quran (Mustafa Khattab): 'Whoever disbelieves in Allah after their belief, not those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith, ...'. The primary text on which the doctrine of coercion (ikrah) and the Oran fatwa's dispensation rest.
sources.license: Scripture; translation by Mustafa Khattab (The Clear Quran) as published on quran.com. Read directly.

sources.citation: al-Wansharisi, Ahmad ibn Yahya. Asna al-matajir fi bayan ahkam man ghalaba 'ala watanihi al-Nasara wa-lam yuhajir, ed. Husayn Mu'nis. Cairo: Maktabat al-Thaqafa al-Diniyya, 1406/1986 (the fatwa is also preserved in al-Wansharisi's collection al-Mi'yar al-mu'rib). Primary Maliki legal text: the question about Andalusian emigrants who regretted their emigration, stating the aim of hijra as 'salamat al-din wa-l-ahl wa-l-walad' and leaving the rule of the unbelieving community; the answer that 'al-hijra min ard al-kufr ila ard al-Islam farida ila yawm al-qiyama', lapsing only for those unable in every way (Q 4:97-99); the quotation of Ibn Rushd al-Jadd against residing 'haythu tajri 'alayhi ahkam al-mushrikin'; and the colophon dated 19 Dhu l-Qa'da 896. The Islamic legal primary-text lens. Read directly for these passages in the OpenITI digital text (from al-Maktaba al-Shamila, based on Mu'nis's edition).
sources.license: Underlying text public domain (1491); digital transcription by OpenITI (open data). Read directly for the passages cited.

sources.citation: Olson, Caitlyn. Review of Jocelyn Hendrickson, Leaving Iberia: Islamic Law and Christian Conquest in North West Africa. Al-Qanṭara 44, no. 1 (2023): e14. doi:10.3989/alqantara.2023.014. Scholarly review summarizing Hendrickson's arguments: that al-Wansharisi's answers in Asna al-matajir and the Marbella fatwa emphasize the obligation to emigrate and were addressed primarily to fellow Maghribi jurists with the Maghribi situation in view, and that al-Wahrani's text was, tentatively, 'unsolicited advice' rather than a fatwa, sent in response to the community's appeal to the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II. Read directly (open access); used for Hendrickson's arguments as summarized, not as an independent source on the fatwas.

Poutrin, Isabelle. 'La conversion des musulmans de Valence (1521-1525) et la doctrine de l'Église sur les baptêmes forcés.' Revue historique 648 (2008): 819-855. doi:10.3917/rhis.084.0819. Peer-reviewed article on the baptisms of Valencian Muslims during the Germanías revolt (summer 1521), Charles V's decree of 1525, on the advice of an assembly of jurists and theologians, that they were valid, and Fernando de Loazes's Tractatus super nova paganorum conversione (1525), which argued their validity under the canonists' doctrine on forced baptism; the outside-scholarship lens on the Christian theological-legal position. Verified to exist and be on-topic through the HAL record (hal-01470936), whose published abstract was read; the body was not read.
